summary:
Cosmic Rescue: The Little Space War is an original browser-based educational space-mission design game developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Players design and manage rescue missions by selecting spacecraft components, including the hull, propulsion, power source, communication antenna, scientific instruments, launch vehicle, and destination.

Every decision involves engineering trade-offs. Powerful instruments may improve scientific discoveries but consume more power, generate more data, or increase spacecraft mass. Players must balance resources to ensure mission success.

The game features six mission levels: Earth Orbit, the Moon, Mars, the Asteroid Belt, Saturn, and an Alien Base. Each level introduces real-world space challenges such as gravity assists, dust storms, radiation risks, solar-power limitations, communication delays, and limited data storage.

Players can participate individually or collaborate in squads of up to four members, taking on four roles: Commander, Engineer, Scientist, and Communications Officer.

A scoring system evaluates rescue success, scientific value, resource efficiency, spacecraft survival, and teamwork. After each mission, players receive a detailed mission report explaining their outcomes and major decisions.

Using NASA's publicly available resources, the game incorporates authentic mission information, planetary facts, imagery, and reference links.
details:
Cosmic Rescue: The Little Space War is an interactive space-mission design and rescue game built as a responsive web application.

Players begin by selecting a squad role: Commander, Engineer, Scientist, or Communications Officer. Up to four players can collaborate on one shared screen. Each role represents a different mission priority, encouraging discussion and negotiation.

Next, players design a spacecraft in a tactical mission-control interface. They select a destination, hull, propulsion system, power system, communications antenna, scientific instruments, and launch vehicle. The game calculates the effects of these choices on budget, mass, electrical power, data storage, fuel, science value, rescue capability, mission time, risk, and armor.

A spacecraft can launch only when it satisfies the launch vehicle’s mass capacity, remains within budget, has enough power for its systems, has sufficient data storage, can reach the selected destination, and includes at least one instrument. If a design fails, the game explains exactly which constraint was violated.

After launch, players travel through six levels: Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars, the asteroid belt, Saturn, and the alien base. Each level presents a NASA-informed clue and three tactical choices. Choices affect fuel, power, data, time, risk, science, rescue progress, and armor. Dangerous choices can cause mission failure if fuel, power, or armor reaches zero, or if cumulative risk becomes too high.

The game includes a tactical HUD with animated resource bars, alerts, mission status, squad roles, and a minimap. It also includes a canvas-based deep-space travel animation, animated planets, a launch countdown, damage effects, and a rescue-victory animation. Browser-generated sound effects use the Web Audio API, so no external audio files are required.

NASA resources are integrated through Mission Intel cards. The game uses the NASA Image and Video Library API for mission imagery, NASA’s APOD API, NASA’s NeoWs API for near-Earth-object context, NASA’s Mars Rover Photos API, and NASA’s EPIC Earth-observation API. Planetary facts and source links are included through NASA Science and NASA’s Planetary Fact Sheets. If live API access fails, the game uses cached fallback imagery so the mission remains playable.

The intended impact is to make space-mission engineering accessible to students and first-time space enthusiasts. Instead of treating mission design as abstract theory, players experience how one decision affects many systems. For example, adding a scientific instrument may increase science value but also increase mass, power use, cost, and data generation.

The project was built with React 18, Vite, JavaScript, CSS, HTML5 Canvas, and the Web Audio API. It is deployed as a static web application and can run without a backend, database, or user login.

The team considered accessibility, mobile responsiveness, educational clarity, replayability, collaboration, originality, and responsible use of NASA data. All characters, story elements, artwork, interface design, sound design, and gameplay systems are original. Data and imagery are courtesy of NASA. This project is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by NASA.
